Joel Palathinkal introduces Mike Ma, delving into his entrepreneurial journey and the balance between parenthood and business. They explore Mike's early life, education, and tech experiences, highlighting his venture capital insights with Next Cubed. The conversation covers investment focus, growth strategies for startups, and insight-driven marketing approaches. Joel and Mike discuss the importance of organic versus paid marketing, effective tactics in sales and fundraising, and the significance of client education. They touch on startup fundamentals, client-centric solutions, and connecting with Limited Partners. The episode concludes with insights on navigating fundraising challenges, best practices, and achieving work-life balance.

The Feedback Loop
Ep. 39: How VCs REALLY Judge Your Startup
Season 1, Ep. 40
•
Monday, November 4, 2024
How do venture capitalists REALLY think through a startup pitch? Well, today is Episode 039 of you getting to find out, as we get to hear pitches from 3 startup founders and see 2 investors react in real-time.
If you're interested in startups and founders building the future, and the venture capitalists funding them, this is a must watch. And today, we hear from founders across personalized skincare (can we finally get over all the conflicting advice on TikTok?), AI-driven nutritional tracking (our investor wants this for his gym bro son), and experiential employee benefits (can this fix our loneliness epidemic, or at least make a dent?).
It's Episode 039 of The Feedback Loop, and it's a fun one!
Pitch 1 (VAIN)
Pitch 2 (Acurixx)
Pitch 3 (ANI)
As always, hosted by Sherveen Mashayekhi, Founder & CEO of Free Agency. ​Today's guest investor, returning to the show for the FIFTH time, was Mike Ma of Sidecut Ventures.
The Feedback Loop is all about getting ambitious founders on stage to pitch and get unfiltered feedback from experienced, honest investors.
Because the thing that can hold even the best founders back from reaching their ambition? Their pitch. Whether a startup founder is raising money, recruiting a team, or selling their product, it's the pitch at the start of any given conversation that starts them on a journey to success.
For those founders on stage and in the audience, it's an answer to the essential query: how to pitch your startup.
More on our guest investor for the episode:
​​Mike is a tech CMO turned venture investor — he runs Sidecut Ventures, backing mission-driven pre-seed founders, and is an Operating Partner at Sway Ventures. He was previously MD at Nex Cubed, a pre-seed accelerator for underrepresented founders. In other words, he knows startup storytelling!
Follow Sherveen: https://x.com/Sherveen
Follow Mike: https://www.instagram.com/michaelwma
To attend The Feedback Loop in-person or apply to pitch as a founder, head to afterfeedback.com.
Thank you to all of the brave founders who participated in this episode. The Feedback Loop is dedicated to creating an engine of support for startup founders attempting to change the way the earth spins. We're on your side.
Curious as to this episode's takeaways? You'll hear about a lot, including how to think about AI features and staying competitive in the AI-driven app space, how men are stealing their girlfriends' skincare, how to sequence a startup pitch, why a question in a pitch meeting is an invitation, how to bring up your credibility as a founder, the challenges of pitching an innovative idea in a legacy industry, and so much more.
This is purpose-built for startup nerds, tech industry fanatics, future founders, and everyone in between.

Venture capitalists hear a new AI startup pitch every 7.9 seconds (it's a fact, don't look it up though). Can Gregory tell a story about a data advantage that can hold up versus the rest of the market?But what does it take to make an AI company truly venture‑scale?As our panelists note, many founders are pitching GPT‑powered solutions – and investors are tired of “just another chatbot.” Gregory’s challenge is to prove a lasting competitive edge: is it the domain expertise and data, the deeper workflow integrations, or a broader vision that extends well beyond real estate?More on our guest investor for the episode:​Ihar Mahaniok is Managing Partner at Geek Ventures, which he founded in 2021 to support immigrant entrepreneurs building at the pre-seed and seed stage. But will GPT’s rapid evolution make specialized datasets obsolete? Investors weigh how to build a moat in a sector evolving at breakneck speed.AI Wrappers vs. Full Workflows: Embedding an AI agent into the full sales lifecycle might create more stickiness than a point‑solution. The Feedback Loop
EP018: Investors REACT to Startup Pitches
Season 1, Ep. 19

Friday, August 9, 2024
On the latest episode, 3 startup founders pitch their hopes and dreams, then get feedback on their storytelling + concept.
Because the thing that can hold even the best founders back from reaching their ambition? Their pitch. Whether a startup founder is raising money, recruiting a team, or selling their product, it's the pitch at the start of any given conversation that starts them on a journey to success.
As always, hosted by Sherveen Mashayekhi, Founder & CEO of Free Agency. Follow him on X at @Sherveen. Find our guest host, Mike Ma of Sidecut Ventures, on Instagram at @michaelwma.
More on Mike:
​​Mike is a tech CMO turned venture investor — he runs Sidecut Ventures, backing mission-driven pre-seed founders, and is an Operating Partner at Sway Ventures. He was previously MD at Nex Cubed, a pre-seed accelerator for underrepresented founders. In other words, he knows startup storytelling!
To attend The Feedback Loop in-person or apply to pitch as a founder, head to afterfeedback.com.
Thank you to all of the brave founders who participated in this episode. The Feedback Loop is dedicated to creating an engine of support for startup founders attempting to change the way the earth spins. We're on your side.

From Startups Decoded
Episode Description
Mike Ma doesn’t invest in decks. He invests in people.
As Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, Mike works with what he calls “coachable superheroes”, early-stage, mission-driven founders tackling real problems in economic mobility, healthcare, climate, and education.
In this conversation, we unpack what it actually means to be coachable as a founder, why most advice fails in practice, and how real progress happens when coaching, capital, and execution collide. Mike shares lessons from the trenches — blending Fortune 500 experience with venture-backed CXO roles, and explains why the best founders don’t just seek answers, they build judgement.
We also explore Sidecut’s hands-on approach to venture building, the parallels between adaptive sports coaching and startup leadership, and why helping founders unlock potential often means meeting them exactly where they are, not where the pitch says they should be.
This episode is for founders who want fewer platitudes, better questions, and support that actually shows up.

Mike believes the best venture outcomes are built through proximity, trust, and real coaching, not performative advice.

Why the fuck did you start this company? Because this is a dumb ass way to make money. It doesn't matter what the business is. And I ask it with the profanity just to jar them. They go by MoFo and are the team behind Startups Decoded.

For decades, MoFo has helped startups turn complexity into freedom. Learn more at mofo.com. Hello and welcome back to Startups Decoded. My name is Andy Walsh. In today's episode, we're looking at a solid GP, but also something quite specific, which is in the lane of impact, which for my mind gets overlooked too easily. And I'd love to hear a bit more from Mike about that, who was our guest today. Welcome, Mike Marr.

Thank you. It's an honor to be here. We've been working on a long time, so I'm glad we're kicking 2026 off right and finally checking things off the list. So thanks so much for having me on. Of course. And I can tell you, though, you're not the person who has the longest lead time of meeting, saying we're going to do a podcast and then recording. There's still some folks that haven't jumped in yet. So you're not at the top of the naughty list. Good, good. Well, hey, I'm trying to, as long as I'm not the last one, I'm good.
00:02:16
Nice. So I appreciate you joining. We met through a mutual friend, Mike McCombie, a fellow solo GP and fascinating human in his own right, as far as what he invests in. Your thesis is a little different to Mike's, but I would love to be able to hear from you on what you've been working on and a little bit around why you do what you do.
00:02:37
Yeah. So thanks for the time. Sidecut Ventures, we call our thesis as shorthand is we back coachable superheroes. And those two words put together make people their heads turn a little bit. So to unpack that, what we do, coachable refers to the way we deploy capital. And we're a little different. Most VCs say, hey, take our money. We give you all this advice and value add. We flip it.

We give all our advice up front in a 30 day co-operating consulting role. We don't take anything for it. No cash, no comment, just your time. You like us. We like you. We'll give you, you know, we'll back you.
00:03:12
The superheroes refers to the impact part. And we are generalists in impact. We've made investments across climate, education, health care, economic mobility, and then accessibility. When we have a disability startup in our portfolio. So we're looking for people who are warriors for good in the world. And that's what we want to back. We expect that while everyone is chasing, you know, a lot of West Coast hot dot type of things, we're really focused on solving intractable human problems. A lot of those do involve AI, but we view that as a how, not a what. And we think if we keep our eye on the ball about big societal problems, there are going to be more than enough returns for everyone to make plenty of money in DPI through the process.

So that's what, that's, that's, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the, that's the fun. We are one year old. We are, we are, we are returns business. And there's a lot of people who have dual you, I mean, sort of dual missions where they have different bottom lines, like make no mistake. We're, we're in the camp of, we expect to not 3X our fund, but 5 to 10X and be a top decile fund.

So I think that from the GP perspective, I think that there is, there are some who, who are not returns based and they're very open about it. And I think the market, both founders and LPs conflate those two together and don't have, it's hard to discern or not as clear.

So I do think there's a different spectrum of impact investors for a variety of good reasons, right? Some are family foundations, which, you know, the returns aren't as important. On Episode 036 of The Feedback Loop, we hear from founders building in: industrial automation, AI for meditation, and end-to-end encrypted AI!
As always, hosted by Sherveen Mashayekhi, Founder & CEO of Free Agency. ​Today's guest investor, returning to the show for the fourth time, was Mike Ma of Sidecut Ventures.
The Feedback Loop is all about getting ambitious founders on stage to pitch and get unfiltered feedback from experienced, honest investors.
Because the thing that can hold even the best founders back from reaching their ambition? Their pitch. Whether a startup founder is raising money, recruiting a team, or selling their product, it's the pitch at the start of any given conversation that starts them on a journey to success.
For those founders on stage and in the audience, it's an answer to the essential query: how to pitch your startup.
More on our guest investor for the episode:

#52: Advice Before Money: The VC Model Founders Actually Want — With Mike Ma.
Startups Decoded
49m
Mike Ma doesn’t invest in decks. He invests in people.
As Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, Mike works with what he calls “coachable superheroes”, early-stage, mission-driven founders tackling real problems in economic mobility, healthcare, climate, and education.
In this conversation, we unpack what it actually means to be coachable as a founder, why most advice fails in practice, and how real progress happens when coaching, capital, and execution collide. Mike shares lessons from the trenches — blending Fortune 500 experience with venture-backed CXO roles, and explains why the best founders don’t just seek answers, they build judgement.
We also explore Sidecut’s hands-on approach to venture building, the parallels between adaptive sports coaching and startup leadership, and why helping founders unlock potential often means meeting them exactly where they are, not where the pitch says they should be.
This episode is for founders who want fewer platitudes, better questions, and support that actually shows up.

Mike believes the best venture outcomes are built through proximity, trust, and real coaching, not performative advice.

The conversation covers investment focus, growth strategies for startups, and insight-driven marketing approaches. Joel and Mike discuss the importance of organic versus paid marketing, effective tactics in sales and fundraising, and the significance of client education. The importance of understanding and addressing the core problems of customers rather than focusing solely on the product itself.
Building authentic relationships and trust through personalized interactions and co-discovery is crucial in the venture capital and fundraising process.
The role of strategic thinking and human connection remains paramount, even with the advent of advanced tools and technologies in marketing and sales.

Investment Thesis
How We Invest
We have a saying at Sidecut: "If you want to be a good partner, go first." We embody that by working closely with founders for 30 days before writing a check. That's how we run our diligence—by helping founders stay productive while we learn how they operate. If you want to see what this looks like in practice, check out our episode of The Pitch (around the 40-minute mark). It's not always pretty, but it's perfectly imperfect.
Why We Invest
We invest in companies that are going to make the world a better place, not clutter it with software. What this looks like are things like Economic Mobility, Digital Health, Education, and Climate. To dive deeper into why we invest in these sectors, listen to our episode of How I Invest.

Transcript
Mike Ma doesn’t invest in decks. He invests in people.
As Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, Mike works with what he calls “coachable superheroes”, early-stage, mission-driven founders tackling real problems in economic mobility, healthcare, climate, and education.
In this conversation, we unpack what it actually means to be coachable as a founder, why most advice fails in practice, and how real progress happens when coaching, capital, and execution collide. Mike shares lessons from the trenches — blending Fortune 500 experience with venture-backed CXO roles, and explains why the best founders don’t just seek answers, they build judgement.
We also explore Sidecut’s hands-on approach to venture building, the parallels between adaptive sports coaching and startup leadership, and why helping founders unlock potential often means meeting them exactly where they are, not where the pitch says they should be.
This episode is for founders who want fewer platitudes, better questions, and support that actually shows up.

Mike Ma
Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, where he invests in and coaches early-stage, mission-driven founders working on some of society’s hardest problems.
He brings a rare blend of Fortune 500 experience (Bank of America, Vanguard) and venture-backed CXO leadership(including Betterment and Own Up), rolling up his sleeves across product, strategy, and fundraising. Mike believes the best venture outcomes are built through proximity, trust, and real coaching, not performative advice.
Outside startups, Mike is an adaptive snowsports instructor and a former member of PSIA-AASI’s National Adaptive Team, training instructors to teach individuals of all abilities. The same coaching mindset he brings to the slopes, patience, adaptability, and belief in latent potential, underpins his work with founders.
